faq.html: FAQs — Tilli
FAQs
Questions, answered
Everything schools and families ask us most often.
Does the child's data go into an AI system? Which one? Can it be turned off?
See the answer <1>↻</1>
Yes, and you should know exactly how.
Read full answer

AskTilli is the assistant your teachers use. When a teacher asks about a specific child, it draws on that child's assessment record to answer, which is why it can say something useful rather than something generic. That's the entire point of it, and it's the difference between advice for a seven-year-old and advice for your seven-year-old.
It runs on Google's Gemini. Records passed to it are identified by school-assigned ID, not by name.
It can be switched off at school level. If you turn it off, assessment, reports and curriculum all continue exactly as before. You lose the assistant, nothing else.
How much time does this take per teacher, per week?
Assessment is about 3 hours per teacher per term, three times a year.
That's five minutes per child for a class of 35, done as structured observation during normal classroom time, not as evening admin. Across a year, roughly 9 hours.
Curriculum is 30 minutes a week, inside an existing period. No new timetable slot, and the weekly plan is written to be picked up and taught without preparation.
Training is two days before you start. Nothing mandatory after that.

We won't claim this replaces something. In most schools it doesn't. What it does replace is the guesswork in a parent-teacher meeting, and teachers tell us that conversation gets shorter and considerably easier.
We're mid-year. Can we start in January?
Yes, and January is a reasonable time to start.

The one thing that has to happen first is a baseline. Every child is assessed across all twelve skills before any teaching begins, because without it you have activities rather than evidence. That takes the first two to three weeks.

A January start gives you a baseline in January and a second measurement before the year closes. That's one growth comparison in your first year rather than two, which is enough to know whether it's working and enough to take to a management committee.
If you'd rather begin the 36-week curriculum in June and use the intervening months to baseline and train your teachers, we'll do it that way instead. Several schools have.
What do parents actually receive, and how often?
A report on their own child, three times a year, at each assessment point.

It opens with the child by name and covers where they stand across all twelve skills, what's grown since the last report, and two or three specific things to try at home. It's written for a parent, not for a specialist. No jargon, no scores out of ten, no comparison against other children.

Parents also receive a short survey each term, around ten minutes, asking what they see at home. That's one of the three perspectives the assessment draws on, and it's why the report can say something a school report can't.
Reports can be delivered in any language your school wants, and you choose whether they go out through us or through your existing channel.
Is this a curriculum, an assessment, or both?
Both, and you can buy the assessment on its own.
Most schools that start with measurement alone add the curriculum within a year, because once you can see where a cohort is thin, the obvious question is what to do about it.
What we don't sell is the curriculum without the assessment. A programme you can't measure is one you'll stop running by Term 2, and you'd have no way of knowing whether that mattered.
Is there any evidence this works? Where's it published?

Yes. The instrument is validated with 12,510 children, and in partner schools 9 in 10 children improved emotion regulation in a single term. What isn't out yet is a peer-reviewed outcome study, and we'd rather tell you that than show you someone else's research.

Tilli was incubated at Stanford's Graduate School of Education and runs an ongoing research-practice partnership with Stanford. Two papers are in progress: one with Hippocampus Learning Centres for a CASEL special issue, and one on behavioural regulation in Sri Lanka currently in revision. That speaks to how we work. It isn't yet a published outcome study, and we won't dress it up as one.

What we can show you is your own data. Every school gets a baseline in the first weeks and a comparison every term after. Within one year you'll know whether it worked in your school, with your children, which is a better answer than a study conducted somewhere else.
You can see partner-school results on our <1>Success Stories</1> page. We'll send you the peer-reviewed papers the moment they land.
What does this cost for one grade?
One grade for one year, with a full review after Term 1, is our smallest engagement, and it's how most schools start.

Pricing runs ₹1,600 to ₹3,000 per student per year. A single grade sits at the top of that range, because training and setup cost the same whether it's one grade or six. Adding grades brings the per-child figure down.
For a grade of 60 children, one year is around ₹1.8 lakh. For 100 children, around ₹3 lakh.

Pricing depends on how many grades you start with and your class sizes. A single grade costs the most per child, because training and setup cost the same whether it's one grade or six. Adding grades brings the per-child figure down. Book a call and we'll share pricing in your local currency.
These are starting points, not fixed quotes, and we're open to discussing what works for your school. Bring your section sizes to the call and we'll set the number together.
What do I take to my Management Committee?
Three things, and we'll put them together for you before the call.

A <1>school leader one-pager</1> that sets out what Tilli is, what it costs, what it asks of your teachers, and the evidence position in plain terms. A sample dashboard, so they can see what you'll be looking at through the year. And a <2>sample parent report</2>, so they can see what reaches families.
Between them, that's enough to answer the first round of questions a committee asks without you needing us in the room.

Tilli's Safety Toolbox!

We’re currently working with the UNICEF Innovation Fund to create Tilli's Safety Toolbox. It is a three module, play-based learning experience on Social-Emotional Learning for Child Online Safety. The focus of this project is to help parents and caregivers have meaningful conversations with their children and teachers, educators and social workers deliver powerful learning to their students!

Ownership: The content, frameworks, graphics and trademark is owned by Tilli Kids Inc, as an open source tool, our parameters for fair use is outlined within the project charter.<1/> © 2021 Tilli Kids Inc. All Rights Reserved.
Term of Service linked here: <1>Link</1>

This project is open source because we believe in building things together and letting people benefit from and adapt things rather than everybody reinventing their own wheel. Tilli uses games and storytelling to help parents and teachers facilitate fun conversations about life changing topics.

In order to build great content for children’s social wellbeing we rely on anybody willing to contribute. In fact Tilli encourages volunteers to drive this project! So whether you want to extend our code for your own use case or just help out - we welcome any contributions to make this project better and safer!
1. Tilli Web App
Tilli Safety Tool Box comprises of 3 modules:
<1>Module 1:</1> Feelings and Emotions (Launched)
Learn to identify, label and express emotions and feelings
Develop healthy coping strategies to manage big feelings
<1>Module 2:</1> Trust (Launched)
At the core of staying safe is knowing who and what to trust
Understand what trust means, looks, and feels like
Practice tools like the trust circle to make safer choices
<1>Module 3:</1> Digital Safety (WIP)
Understanding internet safety and developing positive habits around safe sharing, noticing red flags, being kind and reaching out to a trusted adult
Our 3 modules (and even the modules you create) can be accessed with a Web browser over the World Wide Web on any mobile device.
Unlike classical game software, browser-based games can be played instantly and do not require a prior installation!
2. Tilli IDE
The IDE (Integrated Development Environment) helps users create, manage, and modify content on the Tilli Web App without the need for specialized technical knowledge.
<1>In simple terms</1> this tool helps you build more modules without needing to write all the code from scratch (or even know how to code at all).
<1>Explore IDE</1>
3. Tilli x Godot

Tilli uses the open-source Godot Engine to power the interactive modules on our web app. Godot makes it possible to design rich, game-like learning experiences using a visual editor — without needing to write every line of code.

With this integration, anyone can build, customize, and manage new Tilli modules quickly and easily. You don’t need to be a programmer — just focus on the experience you want to create, and Godot takes care of the technical heavy lifting behind the scenes.
